hints: Look closely at the type of glycosidic bond in each polysaccharide. Which ones use alpha-1,4, which use alpha-1,6, and which use beta-1,4?

Remember amylase can only cut alpha-1,4 bonds, so a molecule made only of those bonds will be digested most, one with extra branch bonds will be partly digested, and one with beta bonds will not be digested at all.
walkthrough:
**Recall the bonds in each polysaccharide**

Think of each polysaccharide as a chain of glucose joined in different ways. Cellulose uses beta-1,4 bonds. Amylose is unbranched and uses only alpha-1,4 bonds. Amylopectin uses mostly alpha-1,4 bonds but also has alpha-1,6 bonds at its branch points.

**Apply what amylase can do**

Amylase is very specific and only hydrolyses alpha-1,4 glycosidic bonds. It cannot break beta-1,4 bonds and it cannot break alpha-1,6 branch point bonds. Complete digestion means every bond is broken.

**Match digestion level to structure**

Cellulose has no alpha-1,4 bonds, so no digestion (-). Amylose has only alpha-1,4 bonds, so most digestion (++). Amylopectin has many alpha-1,4 bonds but the alpha-1,6 branches stop complete digestion, so some digestion (+). That combination is row B.

options.A: Cellulose as (-) is correct, but amylopectin cannot be (++) because its alpha-1,6 branches cannot be cut by amylase.
options.B: Correct. Cellulose (-) has only beta-1,4 bonds, amylopectin (+) has alpha-1,4 plus uncut alpha-1,6 branches, amylose (++) has only alpha-1,4 bonds.
options.C: Incorrect because cellulose cannot show (+) digestion as amylase cannot break beta-1,4 bonds, and amylose should show most not no digestion.
options.D: Incorrect because cellulose cannot show (++) digestion and amylopectin shows some not no digestion.
